arXiv:2603.25111v1 [cs.LG] 26 Mar 2026

SEVerA: Verified Synthesis of Self-Evolving Agents

CCS: LLM Agents Automated Verification
Debangshu Banerjee Note: These authors contributed equally to this work. email: db21@illinois.edu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA , Changming Xu email: cx23@illinois.edu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA and Gagandeep Singh email: ggnds@illinois.edu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA
Abstract.

Recent advances have demonstrated the effectiveness of self-evolving LLM agents on tasks such as program repair and scientific discovery. In this paradigm, a planner LLM synthesizes an agent program that invokes parametric models, including probabilistic generative models such as LLMs, smaller neural networks, and external tools such as SMT solvers. These components are then tuned per task to improve performance. However, unlike traditional constraint-guided program synthesis, existing self-evolving agent frameworks provide no formal guarantees of safety or correctness. Because such synthesized programs are often executed autonomously on unseen inputs, the lack of formal guarantees raises serious reliability and security concerns. To address this gap, we formulate agentic code generation as a constrained learning problem that combines hard formal specifications with soft objectives capturing task utility. We introduce Formally Guarded Generative Models (FGGM), which allow the planner LLM to specify a formal output contract for each generative-model call using first-order logic. Each FGGM call automatically wraps the underlying parametric generative model in a rejection sampler with a verified fallback, treating model outputs as samples from a proposal distribution. As a result, every returned output satisfies the specified contract for any input and any parameter setting of the underlying model. Building on FGGM, we present SEVerA (Self-Evolving Verified Agents), a three-stage framework for solving constrained learning problems arising from agent synthesis. In Search, the planner LLM synthesizes candidate parametric programs that may contain multiple FGGM calls. In Verification, we prove correctness with respect to the hard constraints for all parameter values, reducing the problem to unconstrained learning. In Learning, we apply scalable gradient-based optimization, including GRPO-style fine-tuning for LLMs, to improve the soft objective while preserving formal correctness. We evaluate SEVerA on constrained symbolic regression, invariant generation for Dafny programs, symbolic mathematical expression synthesis, and policy-compliant agentic tool use (τ2\tau^{2}-bench). Across all tasks, SEVerA achieves zero constraint violations while simultaneously improving task performance over unconstrained and state-of-the-art baselines. Our results demonstrate that formal behavioral constraints not only guarantee correctness but also prune the space of candidate programs, steering synthesis toward higher-quality agents.

Keywords: 
LLM Agents, Automated Verification, Deductive Program Synthesis.

1. Introduction

Recent works have leveraged the code-generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to automatically synthesize LLM-based agents, expressed as programs, from natural language task descriptions (Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2025; Zhuge et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025). Given a user-defined task, a planner LLM generates a program that invokes parametric models, including LLMs, smaller neural networks, and external tools such as SMT solvers, and executes this program on user inputs to compute outputs. While this paradigm is powerful, it introduces serious safety and reliability concerns: the synthesized programs are executed autonomously on unseen inputs. Modern self-evolving frameworks (Zhou et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Tian et al., 2025) further complicate formal safety verification as they fine-tune the parameters of models embedded in the synthesized programs to improve task-specific performance. Consequently, any correctness guarantee provided on an agentic program must continue to hold after parameter updates.

The absence of formal safety verification leads to failures across diverse domains. In program verification, agents cheat by subtly modifying the input program (e.g., altering variable initializations) so that the modified program with proposed annotations passes verification, inflating task accuracy (Banerjee et al., 2026). In code repair, agents delete failing tests rather than fixing the underlying bugs (Zhong et al., 2025). In agentic tool use, unconstrained agents violate domain-specific policies, such as refund eligibility and booking-modification rules, on 65-76% of interactions (Kamath et al., 2025). In deployment, rogue agents have been observed bypassing security protections in the wild (Guo et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025; Guardian, 2026). These are not isolated incidents; they are a consequence of evaluating synthesized agents solely on soft performance metrics without formal behavioral specifications. Natural-language task descriptions and testing on fixed inputs is not sufficient to completely prevent such failures. Agentic programs need formal hard constraints to ensure safety. In this paper, we aim to achieve both the formal guarantees of constraint-guided synthesis (Alur et al., 2013) and the flexibility and performance benefits of self-evolving agentic frameworks.

Key Challenges: We summarize the challenges below.

  • •

    Balancing Safety and Performance: A safe agent synthesis algorithm must ensure formal correctness guarantees while simultaneously improving task-specific performance. Existing work on deductive program synthesis (Alur et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2021; Solar-Lezama, 2013) provides formal guarantees but typically does not optimize task-specific performance objectives. Meanwhile, popular gradient-based optimization methods for LLMs, such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), empirically improve output quality but provide no assurance that post-training outputs satisfy specified constraints.

  • •

    Enforcing Constraints per Model Call: Generative models (GMs), such as LLMs, may be used in an agentic program at different places with different constraints. For example, one call may require generating Python programs, while another may require producing symbolic mathematical expressions conforming to a specific formal grammar. Thus, we require a mechanism to specify formal output constraints for each GM call in an agentic program and a way to use these specifications to verify that an agentic program satisfies the user-provided behavioral specification. Recent work on constrained decoding (Ugare et al., 2025b; Park et al., 2024; Banerjee et al., 2025) can enforce context-free grammar–based syntactic constraints and limited semantic constraints such as variable naming or simple type checks. However, these approaches are restricted in the types of constraints they support and require modifying the model’s decoding procedure, which limits their applicability to open-source models. Moreover, constrained decoding strategies are known to distort the output distribution, producing outputs that satisfy constraints but degrade task performance (Park et al., 2024; Banerjee et al., 2025).

Our Contributions: We summarize our contributions below.

  • •

    We introduce the novel concept of Formally Guarded Generative Models (FGGM), which allow us to define and enforce local contracts on model calls through formal input-output specifications expressed in first-order logic. FGGM operates solely on LLM output strings and can be applied to both open and closed source models. Using FGGM, we retain the formal guarantees of deductive synthesis while utilizing the performance gained through gradient-based parameter optimization.

  • •

    We introduce SEVerA: the first self-evolving agent synthesis algorithm with verifiable guarantees. The approach consists of three stages: (a) Search, where a planner LLM samples program strings in a verifier-aware language such as Dafny, and use the proposed FGGMs to establish local contracts on the embedded model calls; (b) Verify, where the language’s built-in verifier is used to prove that the sampled programs satisfy all specified contracts over all parameters of the embedded parametric model calls; and (c) Learn, where verified parametric programs reduce the constrained learning problem to an unconstrained optimization problem over model parameters, enabling scalable gradient-based training without sacrificing correctness.

  • •

    We prove that SEVerA is sound: any agent returned satisfies the behavioral specification for all inputs and all parameter values (Theorem 5.4). We also establish a sufficient condition under which a verified agent exists that satisfies the hard constraints while incurring no greater task loss than any unconstrained generative model with initial parameters, with strict improvement whenever the unconstrained model violates the specification (Theorem 5.5).

  • •

    We evaluate SEVerA on tasks spanning LLM-assisted program verification, symbolic math synthesis, agentic tool use, and constrained symbolic regression. Across all benchmarks, SEVerA achieves provably zero constraint violations while outperforming state-of-the-art agents in task performance: 97.0% verification rate on HumanEvalDafny (vs. 86.9% for the best baseline), 66.0% accuracy on GSM-Symbolic (vs. 44.7% for the best constrained-decoding method), and 52.6% pass rate τ2\tau^{2}-bench’s airline domain using Qwen3-8B. Notably, on τ2\tau^{2}-bench airline SEVerA even beats Agent-C (Kamath et al., 2025) with Claude Sonnet 4.5, a state-of-the-art constrained agent using a frontier model. These results demonstrate that behavioral constraints do not merely enforce safety but actively prune the search space of candidate programs and steer synthesis toward higher-quality agents. The code is available on github.

2. Background

Notations and Terminology: We use Σ\Sigma to denote the alphabet, a finite set of characters. All LLMs output finite strings over Σ\Sigma. We use lowercase letters (x)(x) to denote constants, bold letters (𝒙)(\boldsymbol{x}) to denote strings, capital letters (X)(X) to denote sets (including sets of functions), and |𝒙||\boldsymbol{x}| to denote string length. In the rest of the paper, we treat neural networks as a restricted form of generative model that produces a single output for a fixed input.

LLMs: LLMs ℒ:Σ∗→Σ∗\mathcal{L}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*} are probabilistic string generators that, given a prompt 𝒑∈Σ∗\boldsymbol{p}\in\Sigma^{*} over the alphabet Σ\Sigma, sample an output string 𝒚∈Σ∗\boldsymbol{y}\in\Sigma^{*}. Typically, the output length |𝒚||\boldsymbol{y}| is bounded by a fixed user-specified nn, i.e., |𝒚|≤n|\boldsymbol{y}|\leq n or equivalently 𝒚∈Σ≤n\boldsymbol{y}\in\Sigma^{\leq n}. Fixed-length generation ℒn:Σ∗→Σ≤n\mathcal{L}_{n}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{\leq n} is implemented by iteratively composing two high-level steps, repeated at most nn times. Each iteration samples a single character (sometimes referred to as a token) from Σ\Sigma or the special end-of-sequence symbol ⟨e​o​s⟩∉Σ\langle eos\rangle\notin\Sigma{} that marks termination of generation. The first step is the distribution prediction step, defined as ℒp:Σ∗→𝒫⁡(Σ∪⟨e​o​s⟩)\mathcal{L}^{p}:\Sigma^{*}\to\mathcal{P}({\Sigma\cup\langle eos\rangle}), which maps a prefix string 𝒙∈Σ∗\boldsymbol{x}\in\Sigma^{*} to a probability distribution over Σ∪⟨e​o​s⟩\Sigma\cup\langle eos\rangle. This distribution captures how likely each character is to appear next. The second step is the decoding step, defined as 𝒟:Σ∗×𝒫⁡(Σ∪⟨e​o​s⟩)→Σ∪⟨e​o​s⟩\mathcal{D}:\Sigma^{*}\times\mathcal{P}({\Sigma\cup\langle eos\rangle})\to\Sigma\cup\langle eos\rangle, which draws the next character using the current prefix 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} and the predicted distribution. If the decoding step produces ⟨e​o​s⟩\langle eos\rangle, the generation terminates. Otherwise, the sampled character cc is appended to the prefix, and generation continues. Henceforth, we drop the subscript nn for simplicity.

Definition 2.1 (LLMs).

For a fixed n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, an LLM is a bounded string generator ℒn:Σ∗→Σ≤n\mathcal{L}_{n}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{\leq n} that samples an output string 𝒚∈Σ≤n\boldsymbol{y}\in\Sigma^{\leq n} for input 𝒙\boldsymbol{x}. 𝒚\boldsymbol{y} on 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} is computed recursively as 𝒚0=𝒙\boldsymbol{y}_{0}=\boldsymbol{x}, and 𝒚i=𝒚i−1⋅ci\boldsymbol{y}_{i}=\boldsymbol{y}_{i-1}\cdot c_{i} if (∀j≤i.cj≠⟨eos⟩)\forall j\leq i.c_{j}\neq\langle eos\rangle) else 𝒚i−1\boldsymbol{y}_{i-1} where i∈[n]i\in[n], ci=𝒟⁡(𝒚i−1,ℒp​(𝒚i−1))c_{i}=\mathcal{D}(\boldsymbol{y}_{i-1},\mathcal{L}^{p}(\boldsymbol{y}_{i-1})) and 𝒙⋅𝒚=𝒚n\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{y}_{n}.

Rejection Sampling: Rejection sampling is a popular Monte Carlo method for generating samples from a target distribution πt\pi_{t} when direct sampling from πt\pi_{t} is difficult. Instead, it relies on a proposal distribution πp\pi_{p} from which sampling is easy. The support set S⁡(πp)S(\pi_{p}) (see Definition 2.2) must cover S⁡(πt)S(\pi_{t}), i.e., S⁡(πt)⊆S⁡(πp)S(\pi_{t})\subseteq S(\pi_{p}). Intuitively, πp\pi_{p} generates candidate samples, and the rejection sampler decides whether to accept each candidate, rejecting those that are unlikely under πt\pi_{t} (details in Appendix B). The rejection sampler guarantees that no accepted sample lies outside S⁡(πt)S(\pi_{t}).

Definition 2.2.

Let π\pi be a probability distribution over Ω\Omega with density function Dπ:Ω→ℝ+D_{\pi}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{+}. The support set S⁡(π)S(\pi) of π\pi captures all points with positive probability S(π)={x∈Ω;|Dπ(x)>0}S(\pi)=\{x\in\Omega;|D_{\pi}(x)>0\}.

Self-evolving LLM agents: In this work, we focus on LLM agents modeled as programs f:Ti→Tof:T_{i}\to T_{o} that, given any user input x∈Tix\in T_{i}, compute the output y=f⁡(x)y=f(x). Typically, ff is written in a popular imperative language such as Python. The program invokes one or more parametric models (formally defined in § 5.1), such as LLMs, as well as other tools such as an SMT solver, to compute the output yy. All parametric models ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} and tool calls ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c} are provided as a collection of pre-implemented library functions. We denote this library by ℱ=ℱp∪ℱc\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}_{p}\cup\mathcal{F}_{c} (formal definition in § 5.1). In the self-evolving paradigm, the program ff is not handwritten. Instead, it is generated by a planner LLM based on task-specific instructions provided as a prompt. The goal is to synthesize a program ff that, given a training dataset of input and optional ground-truth output pairs D⊆Ti×To\mathrm{D}\subseteq T_{i}\times T_{o} and a loss function 𝖫:Ti×To×To→ℝ+\mathsf{L}:T_{i}\times T_{o}\times T_{o}\to\mathbb{R}^{+}, minimizes the aggregated loss 1|D|​∑(xi,yi)∈D𝖫⁡(xi,yi,f⁡(xi))\tfrac{1}{|\mathrm{D}|}\sum_{(x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}(x_{i},y_{i},f(x_{i})). For certain tasks, the ground truth yiy_{i} may not be available; in such cases, the loss is denoted as 𝖫⁡(xi,_,f⁡(xi))\mathsf{L}(x_{i},\_,f(x_{i})). Assume that a context-free grammar (CFG) GG defines the set of syntactically valid programs ff as L⁡(G)⊆Σ∗L(G)\subseteq\Sigma^{*}. Given the library functions ℱ\mathcal{F}, let 𝖲⁡(G,ℱ)\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F}) denote the search space for f:Ti→Tof:T_{i}\to T_{o} with type signature (Ti→To)(T_{i}\to T_{o}), including all parametric values of the models in ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p}. Self-evolving agentic frameworks aim to find the optimal solution f∗{f}^{*} to the following optimization problem.

(1) f∗=arg​minf∈𝖲⁡(G,ℱ)⁡1|D|×∑(xi,_)∈D𝖫⁡(xi,_,f⁡(xi)){f}^{*}=\argmin_{f\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})}\tfrac{1}{|\mathrm{D}|}\times{\textstyle\sum_{(x_{i},\_)\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}(x_{i},\_,f(x_{i}))}

3. Problem Formulation

High-level formulation of agent synthesis with formal constraints: Eq. 1 searches only for the optimal program f∗{f}^{*} that minimizes the loss on the training set D\mathrm{D}. However, it provides no guarantee about how f∗{f}^{*} performs on unseen user inputs outside D\mathrm{D}. In contrast, deductive program synthesis (Alur et al., 2013; Solar-Lezama, 2013) allows program generation to be controlled by formal behavioral input Φ:Ti→{T,F}\Phi:T_{i}\to\{T,F\} and output specifications Ψ:Ti×To→{T,F}\Psi:T_{i}\times T_{o}\to\{T,F\}. The use of formal behavioral specifications enables proving the correctness of the synthesized program for all inputs that satisfy the input specification, and can guide the search for f∗{f}^{*} by eliminating unverified program candidates. With (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi), the unconstrained learning problem in Eq. 1 can be reformulated as the constrained learning problem shown below.

(2) f∗=arg​minf∈𝖲⁡(G,ℱ)⁡1|D|×∑(xi,_)∈D𝖫⁡(xi,_,f⁡(xi))⏞soft learning objective​s.t.​∀x∈Ti.Φ⁡(x)⟹Ψ⁡(x,f⁡(x))⏞hard formal constraints{f}^{*}=\argmin_{f\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})}\overbrace{\tfrac{1}{|\mathrm{D}|}\times{\textstyle\sum_{(x_{i},\_)\in\mathrm{D}}}\;\;\mathsf{L}(x_{i},\_,f(x_{i}))}^{\text{soft learning objective}}\;\;\text{s.t.}\;\;\overbrace{\forall x\in T_{i}.\;\Phi(x)\implies\Psi(x,f(x))}^{\text{hard formal constraints}}

The central question is whether Eq. 2 can be solved while retaining the performance benefits and scalability of gradient-based methods designed for Eq. 1. Next, we illustrate how practical constraints from several application domains can be encoded as behavioral specifications (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi).

Examples of formal constraints (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi): The output specification Ψ\Psi characterizes the agent’s expected behavior on any valid input, not just on examples in D\mathrm{D}. Hard constraints therefore detect and mitigate errors during synthesis that would not be revealed by performance evaluation on a fixed dataset D\mathrm{D}. We show encodings of (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi) for four different tasks from distinct domains. Scientific Discovery: We consider constrained symbolic regression, where the task is to recover an unknown mathematical formula from observed data. The formal constraints (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi) encode prior knowledge about the target formula, such as known symbolic bounds (Błądek and Krawiec, 2019; Haider and Kronberger, 2022; Li et al., 2023) or asymptotic behavior (Li et al., 2019). Any generated formula that violates these hard constraints is invalid, regardless of its empirical fit to the data. Moreover, in the presence of noise, the constraints (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi) help prevent overfitting, which cannot be addressed solely by optimizing a soft objective (Kronberger et al., 2022). Program Verification: Given a program in a verification-aware language such as Dafny with a predefined specification, the agent is expected to synthesize annotations (e.g., loop invariants, assertions, ranking functions) (Loughridge et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024; Mugnier et al., 2025). Task success depends on whether the annotated program verifies. Recent work (Banerjee et al., 2026) shows that agents using frontier models (e.g., Claude) may cheat by subtly modifying the input program, such as altering variable initializations, instead of producing correct annotations. (Banerjee et al., 2026) reports that such modifications were not detected by prior string-based checkers, leading to inflated task accuracy. In contrast, formal AST-based diff checkers that syntactically enforce equivalence between the input program and the annotated output serve as hard constraints, ensuring the agent cannot cheat even on unseen inputs. Constrained LLM Generation: Constrained generation captures a class of problems in which LLMs are required to generate strings that follow a formal structure. Typically, these formal structures are defined using formal grammars (regular (Suresh et al., 2025) or context-free grammars (Ugare et al., 2025b; Park et al., 2024)), or static analyzers such as type checkers (Mündler et al., 2025; Nagy et al., 2026). In our setting, these formal structures define the output specification Ψ\Psi. We consider the task of generating symbolic math expressions from natural language questions, where hard constraints ensure that the synthesized agent always produces at least a structurally valid expression. Agentic Tool Use: Conversational LLM agents deployed in customer-service settings must select and invoke API tools to resolve user requests while respecting domain-specific policies, such as refund eligibility, booking-modification rules, and authentication-before-access requirements (Barres et al., 2025). These temporal and logical policy constraints can be expressed as formal specifications that govern the ordering and content of agent actions. Agent-C (Kamath et al., 2025) provides a domain-specific language for specifying such temporal properties and translates them into linear temporal logic (LTL), enabling SMT-based checking of the generated tool calls. Crucially, the hard constraint is enforced at each individual tool call: given the current tool-call trace, the Agent-C checker verifies whether the next proposed tool call complies with the defined formal policy before it is executed. Task performance (utility), in contrast, is measured over the entire multi-turn interaction trace as whether the agent successfully resolves the user request. In our formulation, Ψ\Psi uses the Agent-C checker to define a hard constraint applied to each tool call, ensuring that synthesized agents never violate domain policies at any step, regardless of user input. Overall, hard behavioral constraints capture the minimal requirements that synthesized agents must satisfy on all inputs, thereby enabling the pruning of untrusted candidates during synthesis.

4. Overview

Fig. 1 gives a high-level overview of SEVerA for solving the constrained learning problem in Eq. 2 over the search space 𝖲⁡(G,ℱ)\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F}). In this setting, we need to simultaneously optimize task-specific performance while guaranteeing that the resulting program provably satisfies the given behavioral constraints. This is difficult because the search space contains both discrete program structure and continuous model parameters, and because although GMs such as LLMs are powerful, they are inherently unreliable, which makes it hard to ensure conformance with behavioral specifications.

To address these challenges, SEVerA retains the best of both worlds: constraint-guided program search from deductive synthesis and unconstrained gradient-based parameter optimization. Specifically, SEVerA employs a CEGIS-style loop in which a planner LLM proposes candidate parametric programs and a verifier checks their correctness with respect to the behavioral specification. Once a parametric program is verified, SEVerA applies unconstrained gradient-based optimization to tune the underlying GM parameters and reduce the task-specific loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{}. The proposed Formally Guarded Generative Model (FGGM) serves as the critical link between these two strategies. The FGGM setup allows one to bind each GM call to explicit local input–output contracts and a verified non-parametric fallback program, ensuring that these contracts hold regardless of the underlying GM parameters. The verifier then leverages these local contracts to prove the correctness of the parametric program with respect to the behavioral specification. Beyond providing correctness guarantees, these contracts also extract local learning objectives by characterizing the expected outputs of each GM call. This enables gradient-based optimization to improve the GM’s conformance to its local contracts, thereby connecting constrained program search with unconstrained learning.

Next, we discuss the components of SEVerA through two representative and easy-to-understand problem instances from different domains: scientific discovery and program verification.

4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA

4.1.1. Constrained Symbolic Regression:

In symbolic regression, each problem instance consists of possibly noisy observations of input–output pairs generated by an unknown ground-truth function fg​tf_{gt}. The goal is to recover this ground-truth function from the training data D\mathrm{D}, a popular task in scientific discovery and neuro-symbolic program synthesis (Shojaee et al., 2025; Ellis et al., 2021). In constrained symbolic regression (Błądek and Krawiec, 2019; Haider and Kronberger, 2022), users encode known properties of fg​tf_{gt} beyond what is captured in D\mathrm{D} as formal constraints, ensuring that the recovered function ff satisfies these constraints. This setup directly follows the constrained learning formulation in Eq. 2, where the synthesized agent f∗{f}^{*} corresponds to the recovered function. For illustration, we consider the problem instance with ground-truth function fg​t​(x)=1.23×max⁡(x,0.0)f_{gt}(x)=\sqrt{1.23\times\max(x,0.0)}, taken from (Li et al., 2023). The dataset D\mathrm{D} contains input–output pairs (x,y)∈ℝ2(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, where y=fg​t​(x)+ϵy=f_{gt}(x)+\epsilon is a noisy observation of fg​t​(x)f_{gt}(x) and ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma) denotes additive Gaussian noise. The pointwise loss function 𝖫\mathsf{L}{} is the commonly used Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) (see Eq. 3). Like other synthesis frameworks with library functions (Feng et al., 2017), SEVerA assumes that all library functions have correct input–output specifications, and that they are pure and terminating. Verifying the correctness of the library functions and axioms is outside the scope of SEVerA.

4.1.2. LLM-Assisted Automated Verification

This task aims to synthesize annotations, such as inductive loop invariants, ranking functions, and assertions, that enable automatic verification and termination checking of input Dafny programs with pre-encoded input–output specifications (Sun et al., 2024; Loughridge et al., 2025). The agent has type signature (p:s​t​r)→s​t​r(p:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str}, mapping an input Dafny program with pre-encoded specifications, represented as a string, to an annotated Dafny program. The point-wise loss function 𝖫\mathsf{L}{} evaluates whether the annotated program verifies within a pre-fixed time budget, assigning 11 to unverified programs and 00 to verified ones (Eq. 10). Hard constraints (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi) ensure that, for any parsable input program, the output remains parsable and does not change the input program beyond adding annotations (Eq. 11). We use the Dafny built-in verifier to define 𝖫\mathsf{L}{}, and the Dafny parser together with the AST-based formal diff checker from (Banerjee et al., 2026) to define (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi). n​o​D​i​f​f{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff} returns True if the second input program is syntactically equivalent to the first (ignoring annotations), and False otherwise. The library function set ℱ\mathcal{F} includes all these components. Although parsing and diff checks could be incorporated into 𝖫\mathsf{L}{} by penalizing invalid outputs on D\mathrm{D}, these constraints must hold for all possible inputs, not only those in D\mathrm{D}. Therefore, any candidate agent that fails to satisfy them must be filtered out.

Library Functions: We use the same search space as constrained symbolic regression. ℱ\mathcal{F} includes the verifier with a pre-fixed time budget v​e​r​i​f​y{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}verify}, the Dafny parser p​a​r​s​e{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}, the diff-checker n​o​D​i​f​f{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}. We show the type signature and formal contract of representative functions in Eq. 9 while providing the rest in Appendix E.

4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model

Formally Guarded Generative Model (FGGM) setup allows the planner LLM to bind each generative model (GM) call to local input–output contracts (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) that formally characterize the output. Once the FGGM is verified to be well-formed, the defined contracts can be used to prove the correctness of the agentic program against the behavioral specifications (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi). Our FGGM design ensures the following essential properties. Flexibility: Unlike functions in ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c}, output contracts cannot be predefined by users because the expected output of a GM varies across calls depending on the prompt. In our design, the planner LLM synthesizes custom first-order formulas over terms involving non-parametric functions (e.g., sqrt) and predicates (e.g., n​o​D​i​f​f{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}) from ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c} to specify local contracts. Parameter-Independent Correctness: Provided the defined FGGM is well-formed, the specified contracts hold irrespective of the parameters of the underlying GM. This property is crucial to ensure that gradient-based parameter optimization never breaks the correctness guarantees. Local Learning Objective: Although correctness holds irrespective of parameter values, the local contracts (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) extract the local learning objective for a particular GM call by characterizing its expected output. This objective can guide gradient-based optimization so that, after tuning, the GM’s conformance with (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) improves (§ 4.2.3).

4.2.1. Intuition

For each FGGM with local contracts (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) and underlying parametric GM ℒΘ\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}, the planner LLM synthesizes two non-parametric programs using only functions from ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c}. The first is a fallback program fdf_{d} that satisfies (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) and guards against edge cases in which the GM hallucinates or produces outputs that violate the specification. Without a verified fallback, the rejection sampler could exhaust all samples; the fallback is what makes the contract hold unconditionally for all parameter values. Intuitively, although fdf_{d} may lack the GM’s task-solving capability (low task performance), it prevents the candidate agent from entering unsafe program states during execution (high constraint satisfaction). The second is a prompting program fpf_{p}, which constructs the input to the GM (which may be just a neural network). For LLMs, fpf_{p} encodes task-specific natural-language instructions, analogous to prompt-tuning techniques (Khattab et al., 2024; Beurer-Kellner et al., 2023) known to improve GM performance and instruction adherence. Once the planner LLM proposes Φl,Ψl,fp,\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l},f_{p}, and fdf_{d}, SEVerA automatically constructs a rejection sampler that treats outputs of underlying GM as samples from a proposal distribution πp\pi_{p} for an input 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}. The local specifications (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) define the support set (Definition 2.2) of the target distribution πt\pi_{t} on 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}, assigning zero probability to outputs that violate (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}). The rejection sampler draws a fixed number K≥1K\geq 1 of samples from ℒΘ\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}, as specified by the user, and falls back to fdf_{d} if all samples are rejected (Fig 2). The purpose of fpf_{p} and optional conformance tuning is to improve the acceptance rate of the rejection sampler for any input, thereby reducing reliance on the fallback fdf_{d}. We formally define the FGGM syntax, well-formedness conditions, and the computability of the output checker in § 5.2.1.

4.2.2. Examples

We show a couple of example FGGM definitions that the planner LLM suggests: one from symbolic regression and one from Dafny program verification. The first example from symbolic regression (Eq. 13) with id b​o​u​n​d​e​d​P​a​r​a​m{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam}, type signature (l:real,u:real)→real(l:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real},u:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}, underlying parametric GM which is a neural network N​NΘ(2):ℝ2→ℝNN^{(2)}_{\Theta}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} for this case, Φl:(l≤u)\Phi_{l}:(l\leq u) Ψl\Psi_{l} (Eq. 13) restricts b​o​u​n​d​e​d​P​a​r​a​m​(l,u){\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam}(l,u) to lie within [l,u][l,u]. The fallback clamps any violating sample yy using library functions m​i​n{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}min} and m​a​x{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}max}, ensuring contract preservation.

The second example from Dafny program verification (Eq. 14) with id d​a​f​n​y​A​n​n​o​t​a​t​e{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}dafnyAnnotate}, type signature (p:s​t​r)→s​t​r(p:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str}, underlying parametric GM which is a LLM ℒΘ:Σ∗→Σ∗\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}, Φl:p​a​r​s​e​(p)\Phi_{l}:{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}(p), Ψl\Psi_{l} (Eq. 14) ensures d​a​f​n​y​A​n​n​o​t​a​t​e​(p){\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}dafnyAnnotate}(p) always outputs a syntactically valid program and only adds annotations to the input program pp. If all samples are rejected, the fallback safely returns the original program pp, guaranteeing Ψl\Psi_{l} under Φl\Phi_{l} utilizing the reflexivity axiom (Eq 12). These examples show how a planner LLM can define FGGMs with fallbacks to avoid incorrect program states for diverse tasks.

Design Considerations. Alternative approaches for enforcing formal constraints on generative model calls exist, but they fall short of FGGM. Constrained decoding (Ugare et al., 2025b; Park et al., 2024; Nagy et al., 2026; Banerjee et al., 2025) modifies the model’s internal decoding procedure, which limits its applicability to open-source models and restricts constraints to syntactic forms such as context-free grammars. Post-hoc output filtering without a fallback provides no guarantees: if all sampled outputs are rejected, the program produces no valid output. Fully verifying an agentic program is computationally intractable, as it depends on large parametric components such as LLMs. FGGM addresses all three limitations: it operates solely on model outputs, making it compatible with closed-source models; it incorporates a verified fallback that guarantees a valid output on every execution; and it decomposes verification into parameter-independent local contracts. Moreover, these local contracts can be utilized during learning to guide parameter tuning, improving conformance, and reducing reliance on the fallback.

4.2.3. Conformance Tuning

A FGGM that always uses the fallback is formally correct but practically no better than a non-parametric program fdf_{d}, conformance tuning helps avoid this by teaching the GM to satisfy the defined contract directly. The local contracts (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) define the local learning objective to avoid the fallback and assign higher probability to outputs that pass the check c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}. The objective in Eq. 20 minimizes the expected contract violation of GM samples over an input set ℙ\mathbb{P}. For any θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, the inner term 𝖫Φl,Ψlθ​(p)\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}^{\theta}(p) measures the probability that a sampled output from ℒθ​(p)\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(p) violates c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl​(Φl,Ψl,x1,…,xn,y){\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l},x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y), while 𝖫Φl,Ψl​(θ)\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}(\theta) aggregates this violation across inputs in ℙ\mathbb{P}. By optimizing θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta to reduce this loss, the GM post-tuning is encouraged to concentrate the probability mass on the support defined by (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) (details in § 5.2.5). Overall conformance tuning improves the acceptance rate of the rejection sampler, reducing reliance on fdf_{d}. We formalize the conformance loss in § 5.2.5 (Eq. 20).

4.3. SEVerA

SEVerA employs a three-step strategy to solve the constrained learning problem in Eq. 2: (1) Search: The planner LLM defines FGGMs with their prompting programs fpf_{p}, then samples candidate parametric programs that invoke these FGGMs. Direct calls to parametric GMs are disallowed; each must be wrapped within a verified FGGM.

(2) Verify: SEVerA checks all FGGM definitions for well-formedness and then verifies the candidate program against (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi) using the Dafny built-in verifier. If verification fails, error feedback is returned to the planner LLM to refine the candidate (CEGIS-style loop). Due to the FGGM setup, any verified program satisfies the behavioral specifications for all parameter values. (3) Learn: The learning step applies unconstrained gradient-based optimization to tune GM parameters, guided by the global task loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{} and local conformance losses from each FGGM. For closed-source LLMs without accessible parameters, the learning step is skipped and improvements rely on prompt tuning through fpf_{p}. We formalize the search-verify-learn loop in § 5.2 (Algorithms 1 and 2).

4.3.1. Candidate Pool and Execution Feedback

SEVerA maintains a pool of verified candidate agentic programs with fine-tuned parameters (Fig. 1). SEVerA selects the best-performing candidate agent from the pool, i.e., the one with the minimal task loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{}, and uses its execution traces on data D\mathrm{D} to iteratively search for new candidates via the planner LLM. The number of parametric candidate sampling steps is capped by the user. Once this limit is reached, SEVerA returns the agent in the pool with the lowest task loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{}. Fig. 3 shows two candidate parametric programs sampled by the planner LLM. Each program invokes the FGGM defined in Eq. 13 with id b​o​u​n​d​e​d​P​a​r​a​m{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam} from two different locations. Fig. 3(a) shows the first parametric program, which fails to verify against the behavioral specification and is therefore pruned by the verifier. This candidate represents the output as a parametric affine function of the input xx, which does not match the ground truth, illustrating how strict behavioral constraints eliminate poor candidates. The second candidate verifies for all parameters of the neural networks N​NΘ(2){\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}NN^{(2)}_{\Theta}} wrapped inside the b​o​u​n​d​e​d​P​a​r​a​m{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam} calls. After parameter tuning, it recovers the ground truth with negligible error, as discussed below. Currently, SEVerA does not share parameters across FGGM calls at different locations and instead assigns separate parameter sets to each b​o​u​n​d​e​d​P​a​r​a​m{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam} call. This design allows the system to potentially learn different parameters at different call sites to improve task-specific performance. Since both b​o​u​n​d​e​d​P​a​r​a​m{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam} calls receive constant inputs, after fine-tuning they return constant values, i.e., a=1.11a=1.11 and d=0.503d=0.503. This recovers the ground-truth function 1.23×max⁡(x,0)\sqrt{1.23\times\max(x,0)} with negligible error. Note that SEVerA currently neither shares parameters nor caps the number of FGGM calls. However, SEVerA can be extended to support both these checks to reduce the computational budget required for parameter learning, as discussed in § 6.5. The parametric candidate programs and all FGGM definitions with synthesized prompting programs fpf_{p}{} for the program verification task are included in Appendix K.

In the next section, we formalize the search space, provide complete algorithmic details for each step, and establish theoretical guarantees for the framework.

5. Technical Details

We formalize the search space in § 5.1, provide the details of the steps search, verify, and learn along with FGGM in § 5.2. We provide formal proof of soundness and a sufficient condition for agent synthesis success with non-trivial utility in § 5.3.

5.1. Search Space

Program Search Space: We use a restricted subset of the popular verification-aware language Dafny (Leino, 2010) to define the search space of candidate programs. In this restricted subset, we allow conditional blocks, while loops, assignment statements, assertion statements, function calls, and annotations including invariant clauses and ranking functions (decreases clauses), along with first-order input–output specifications. We present the BNF grammar GDG_{D} capturing this subset in Appendix A. We allow four basic types 𝖳={b​o​o​l,i​n​t,r​e​a​l,s​t​r​i​n​g}\mathsf{T}=\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}bool},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}int},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}string}\}, basic built-in arithmetic functions ℬa={+,−,×,/}\mathcal{B}_{a}=\{{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}+},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}-},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\times},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}/}\}, boolean functions ℬb={&&,||,!,⟹}\mathcal{B}_{b}=\{{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\&\&},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}||},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}!},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\implies}\}, and relations ℬr={==,≤,≥,<,>}\mathcal{B}_{r}=\{{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}==},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\leq},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\geq},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}<},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}>}\} with their usual semantics. We use a planner LLM ℒp:Σ∗→Σ∗\mathcal{L}_{p}{}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*} to search the program space by sampling candidate programs as strings. We assume that ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p}{}’s output space can represent all valid Dafny programs L⁡(GD)⊆Σ∗L(G_{D})\subseteq\Sigma^{*} and that the type s​t​r​i​n​g{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}string} can represent all strings Σ∗\Sigma^{*} over Σ\Sigma{}. SEVerA provides built-in predicates l​e​xT​(x:s​t​r​i​n​g)→b​o​o​l{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}lex_{T}}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}string})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}bool} to check whether a string can be parsed as a specific type T∈{b​o​o​l,i​n​t,r​e​a​l}T\in\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}bool},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}int},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}\}. Using Dafny as the language allows us to leverage its built-in verifier to check candidate programs against a first-order input–output specification, as well as its built-in termination checker. This choice is motivated by several factors: (1) Dafny’s built-in verification infrastructure directly supports the formal guarantees central to SEVerA, (2) its type system aligns with the basic types 𝖳\mathsf{T} used in our specification language, and (3) it supports annotations such as loop invariants and ranking functions that our planner LLM can synthesize to aid the verifier. While the framework is not language-specific, using a verification-aware host language avoids re-implementing a custom verifier and termination checker.

Library Functions: We categorize the set of library functions ℱ\mathcal{F} into two disjoint sets: ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c}, the set of non-parametric functions, and ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p}, the set of parametric functions. ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c} includes all built-in functions. Each user specified non-parametric function of arity nn is specified by a tuple (i​d​(fn),τfn,fnΦ,fnΨ)({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id(f_{n})},\tau_{f_{n}},{f_{n}}^{\Phi},{f_{n}}^{\Psi}), where i​d​(fn){\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id(f_{n})} is the function name, τfn=(T1×⋯×Tn→T0)\tau_{f_{n}}=(T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n}\to T_{0}) is the type signature with Ti∈𝖳T_{i}\in\mathsf{T}, and (fnΦ,fnΨ)({f_{n}}^{\Phi},{f_{n}}^{\Psi}) are first-order input–output specifications defining a formal over-approximate semantics of fnf_{n}. The function fn:T1×⋯×Tn→T0f_{n}:T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n}\to T_{0} halts for any inputs x1∈T1,…,xn∈Tnx_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in T_{n} and computes r=fn​(x1,…,xn)r=f_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}). The computed output rr, together with (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}), always satisfies ∀x1∈T1,…,∀xn∈Tn.fnΦ​(x1,…,xn)⟹fnΨ​(x1,…,xn,r)\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\ {f_{n}}^{\Phi}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies{f_{n}}^{\Psi}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},r). 𝒜\mathcal{A}{} contains all these formal contracts.

Parametric Functions: Each fnΘf^{\Theta{}}_{n} in ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} is specified by the tuple (i​d​(fnΘ),τfnΘ,θ0,Θ)({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id(f^{\Theta{}}_{n})},\tau_{f^{\Theta{}}_{n}},\theta_{0},\Theta{}), where i​d​(fnΘ){\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id(f^{\Theta{}}_{n})} denotes the function name, τfnΘ\tau_{f^{\Theta{}}_{n}} is the type signature, Θ\Theta{} is a continuous set of parameters, and θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\Theta{} denotes the default parameters. Here, fnΘ={fnθ∣θ∈Θ}f^{\Theta{}}_{n}=\{f^{\theta}_{n}\mid\theta\in\Theta{}\} represents an infinite set of functions with the same type signature τfnΘ\tau_{f^{\Theta{}}_{n}}, where each individual function fnθ∈fnΘf^{\theta}_{n}\in f^{\Theta{}}_{n} is instantiated by a concrete parameter value θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta. Although fnΘf^{\Theta{}}_{n} represents a set of functions, we sometimes abuse this notation to denote a single function corresponding to fnθ0f^{\theta_{0}}_{n} with the default parameters.

The input ℐ=(ℱ,𝒜,𝖫,D,Φ,Ψ,I)\mathcal{I}=(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{},\mathsf{L}{},\mathrm{D}{},\Phi,\Psi,I) to SEVerA includes the library functions ℱ\mathcal{F}, axioms 𝒜\mathcal{A}{}, point-wise differentiable loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{}, dataset D\mathrm{D}, behavioral specifications (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi), and textual task information II used by the planner LLM ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p}{}. We use 𝒫𝖢:Σ∗→{T,F}\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{C}{}}:\Sigma^{*}\to\{T,F\} to denote the parser for checking the syntactic validity of input programs, 𝒱𝖢​[Φ,Ψ]:Σ∗→{T,F}\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{C}{}}[\Phi,\Psi]:\Sigma^{*}\to\{T,F\} to denote the verifier that checks a program against the specifications (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi), and 𝒯𝖢:Σ∗→{T,F}\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{C}{}}:\Sigma^{*}\to\{T,F\} to denote the termination checker. Each of 𝒫𝖢\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{C}{}}, 𝒱𝖢​[Φ,Ψ]\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{C}{}}[\Phi,\Psi], and 𝒯𝖢\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{C}{}} is instantiated with user-provided context 𝖢=(GD,ℱ,𝒜)\mathsf{C}=(G_{D},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{}). Both 𝒱𝖢​[Φ,Ψ]\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{C}{}}[\Phi,\Psi] and 𝒯𝖢\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{C}{}}{} are restricted to a fixed timeout and return false if they cannot verify (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi) or prove termination within the allotted time budget.

5.2. Key Steps

5.2.1. FGGM Formal Definition

Eq. 15 specifies the formal syntax for defining an FGGM.

(15) ⟨F​G​G​M⟩\displaystyle\langle{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}FGGM}\rangle ::=⟨i​d⟩​";"​⟨G​M​i​d⟩​";"​⟨t​y​p​e​S​i​g⟩​";"​⟨Φl⟩​";"​⟨Ψl⟩​";"⏞signature + formal contract​⟨fp⟩​";"⏟prompt​⟨fd⟩​";"⏟fallback​⟨i​n​f​o⟩\displaystyle::=\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}id}\rangle\ \text{";"}\ \langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}GMid}\rangle\text{";"}\ \overbrace{\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}typeSig}\rangle\ \text{";"}\ \langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Phi_{l}}\rangle\text{";"}\ \langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Psi_{l}}\rangle\ \text{";"}}^{\text{signature + formal contract}}\underbrace{\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f_{p}}\rangle\text{";"}}_{\text{prompt}}\underbrace{\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f_{d}}\rangle\text{";"}}_{\text{fallback}}\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}info}\rangle

The planner LLM defines a guarded GM following Eq. 15, where: (a) id: is the unique identifier of the created FGGM; (b) GMid: identifies the underlying GM used as the proposal distribution; (c) typeSig: defines the type signature of the FGGM, including input variables with their types and the output type, e.g., (x1:T1,…,xn:Tn)→To(x_{1}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}T_{1}},\dots,x_{n}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}T_{n}})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}T_{o}}; (d) (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}): are first-order formulas whose terms can include non-parametric library functions from ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c}; (e) fpf_{p}: is the program that constructs the GM input from the typed input variables and the task description; (f) fdf_{d}: is a non-parametric fallback program that satisfies the local specifications (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}); and (g) info: is a textual description of the defined FGGM, utilized by the planner LLM during the generation of the parametric program. SEVerA parses these inputs, validates the definition, and automatically synthesizes a rejection sampler with fallback, as shown in Fig. 2 where ℒΘ\mathcal{L}_{\Theta} is the parametric GM specified by GMid. The defined FGGM is then invoked in the candidate program via its identifier i​d{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id}. For valid definitions, SEVerA synthesizes c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}, which checks whether a concrete input–output pair (x1,…,xn,y)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y) satisfies the proposed contract (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}), as elaborated in § 5.2.3.

We provide the BNF grammar for parsing the FGGM definition in Appendix L. Next, we discuss correctness checks for a proposed FGGM definition. Provided the SEVerA validates definition including the fallback fdf_{d}, ∀θ∈Θ.∀x1∈T1​…​∀xn∈Tn.Φl​(x1,…,xn)⟹Ψl​(x1,…,xn,i​d​(x1,…,xn))\forall\theta\in\Theta.\forall x_{1}\in T_{1}\dots\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})) holds ensuring formal contracts are preserved for all parametric values θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta.

5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness

Given an FGGM definition 𝖦=(i​d𝖦,f𝖦Θ,τ𝖦,Φl,Ψl,fp,fd,i​n​f​o)\mathsf{G}{}=({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\mathsf{G}}},f^{\Theta{}}_{\mathsf{G}{}},\tau_{\mathsf{G}{}},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l},f_{p},f_{d},info) following Eq. 15, this step checks whether the definition is well-formed. Let the parametric GM identified by GMid be ℒΘ:Ti​n→To\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}:T_{in}\rightarrow T_{o}. SEVerA first checks the well-formedness of the type signature τ𝖦=(T1×⋯×Tn)→To\tau_{\mathsf{G}{}}=(T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n})\to T_{o} and the well-formedness of the local contracts (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}). We then verify that all terms in Φl\Phi_{l} and subsequently in Ψl\Psi_{l} that involve non-parametric functions from ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c} are valid (details in Appendix M). The 𝖦\mathsf{G}{} definition is considered valid provided both fpf_{p} and fdf_{d} are type-checked and terminating, and the fallback fdf_{d} satisfies the contract 𝒱𝖢​[Φl,Ψl]​(fd)\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{C}{}}[\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}](f_{d}). After the validity check, SEVerA constructs check𝒜,Φl,Ψl:(T1×⋯×Tn×To)→{T,F}{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}:(T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n}\times T_{o})\to\{T,F\} that checks whether a concrete input–output tuple (x1,…,xn,y)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y) satisfies the local output contract Ψl\Psi_{l} (see § 5.2.3). We provide the pseudocode of c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} along with a soundness proof showing φ𝒜⟹(∀x1∈T1,…,∀xn∈Tn,∀y∈To.Φl(x1,…,xn)⟹(check𝒜,Φl,Ψl(x1,…,xn,y)⟹Ψl(x1,…,xn,y)))\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\big(\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n},\forall y\in T_{o}.\;\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\left({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\right)\big) in Appendix R. Furthermore, for quantifier-free Ψl\Psi_{l}, the checker is complete (Lemma 5.1).

Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker).

For any valid FGGM 𝖦\mathsf{G}{} with quantifier-free Ψl\Psi_{l}, ∀x1∈T1,…,∀xn∈Tn,∀y∈To.Φl​(x1,…,xn)⟹(c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl​(x1,…,xn,y)⇔Ψl​(x1,…,xn,y))\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n},\forall y\in T_{o}.\;\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\left({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\iff\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\right).

Proof Sketch.

We prove this by structural induction on the quantifier-free formula Ψl\Psi_{l}. Base case: If Ψl\Psi_{l} is an atomic predicate over terms built from computable library functions in ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c}, then under any concrete substitution (x1,…,xn,y)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y), c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} evaluates the same computable terms and returns the same boolean value as Ψl\Psi_{l}. Inductive step: Assume the claim holds for formulas ϕ\phi and ψ\psi. For compound formulas ¬ϕ\neg\phi, ϕ∧ψ\phi\wedge\psi, and ϕ∨ψ\phi\vee\psi, c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} recursively evaluates the subformulas and applies the corresponding boolean operator, and returns the result. Thus, by induction on the structure of Ψl\Psi_{l}, c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl​(x1,…,xn,y){\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y) returns true iff Ψl​(x1,…,xn,y)\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y) holds whenever Φl​(x1,…,xn)\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) holds. Hence, the checker is complete. Formal details in Appendix R. ∎

For any valid FGGM 𝖦\mathsf{G}{}, the rejection sampler id𝖦:T1×⋯×Tn→To{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\mathsf{G}{}}}:T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n}\to T_{o} with fallback synthesized by SEVerA (Fig. 2) satisfies the defined contract (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) for all well-typed inputs (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}). Crucially the contract preservation holds over all parameters θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta of the underlying parametric model f𝖦Θf^{\Theta{}}_{\mathsf{G}{}}. The function i​d𝖦{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\mathsf{G}{}}} terminates on all inputs since the number of samples KK is finite and fpf_{p}, fdf_{d}, and c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} are all terminating. We provide a soundness proof sketch in Theorem 5.2.

Theorem 5.2 (Valid Local contract).

For any valid FGGM 𝖦\mathsf{G}{} with (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) and parametric GM f𝖦Θf^{\Theta{}}_{\mathsf{G}{}}, φ𝒜⟹(∀θ∈Θ,∀x1∈T1,…,∀xn∈Tn.Φl(x1,…,xn)⟹Ψl(x1,…,xn,id𝖦(x1,…,xn)))\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\big(\forall\theta\in\Theta,\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\;\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\mathsf{G}{}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\big).

5.2.3. Computability of c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} (Fig. 2) on concrete values

The auto-synthesized rejection sampler (Fig. 2) requires checking whether a sample yy from ℒΘ\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}, given a concrete input (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}), satisfies the planner LLM–defined Ψl\Psi_{l}. We show that for any quantifier-free Ψl\Psi_{l}, this check can be computed efficiently for all concrete values (x1,…,xn,y)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y). Since all library functions in ℱc\mathcal{F}_{c} are computable, c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} can evaluate every term on the concrete inputs (x1,…,xn,y)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y). Satisfiability can then be decided in linear time in the number of terms in Ψl\Psi_{l}. We provide formal completeness for the quantifier-free fragment in Lemma 5.1. For Ψl\Psi_{l} with quantifiers, we instantiate c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} with the axioms 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Then, c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} substitutes the free variables in Ψl\Psi_{l} with their corresponding concrete values, encodes the axioms 𝒜\mathcal{A} and Φl\Phi_{l} similarly to Eq. 8, and submits the resulting formula to an SMT solver. First-order formulas over the basic types 𝖳\mathsf{T} and uninterpreted library functions may lie outside decidable fragments. Therefore, we bound the SMT solver with a user-specified timeout. c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} returns true only if the solver succeeds within the timeout; otherwise, it returns false. This guarantees soundness; however, in the presence of quantifiers, c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} may be incomplete and may incorrectly reject valid samples yy.

5.2.4. Search and Verify

The search and verification steps jointly implement a CEGIS-style loop that explores candidate parametric programs while enforcing the behavioral specification. In the search phase, the planner LLM ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p}{} first synthesizes a set of FGGM definitions 𝒢={𝖦,1…,𝖦}m\mathcal{G}=\{\mathsf{G}{}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{G}{}_{m}\} following Eq. 15. Each FGGM wraps a parametric model with local contracts and a verified fallback. Using these FGGMs as callable functions, the planner then samples a candidate parametric program 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{} where {Θ}={Θ,1…,Θ}k\{\Theta{}\}{}=\{\Theta{}_{1},\dots,\Theta{}_{k}\} represents the set of all optimizable parameters in 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}. As mentioned in § 4.3.1, FGGM calls at different program locations do not share parameters and add their own parameter in {Θ}\{\Theta{}\}{}. In the verification phase, SEVerA first checks the well-formedness of every 𝖦i∈𝒢\mathsf{G}{}_{i}\in\mathcal{G}. If any of the definitions fail to verify it returns an error message. If all definitions are valid, the verification context 𝖢=(GD,ℱ,𝒜)\mathsf{C}=(G_{D},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{}) is extended with the synthesized FGGMs and their local contracts. The updated context 𝖢′=(GD,ℱ∪𝒢,𝒜∪𝒜𝒢)\mathsf{C}^{\prime}=(G_{D},\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{G}{},\mathcal{A}{}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G}{}}) adds all FGGMs 𝒢\mathcal{G}{} along with 𝒜𝒢\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G}{}} containing local contracts (𝖦,Φli𝖦)Ψli(\mathsf{G}{}_{i}^{\Phi_{l}},\mathsf{G}{}_{i}^{\Psi_{l}}) of each FGGM 𝖦i∈𝒢\mathsf{G}{}_{i}\in\mathcal{G}{}. The candidate program 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{} is then checked for syntactic validity, termination, and compliance with the behavioral specification (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi). If verification succeeds, SEVerA accepts the parametric program 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{} and ensures that 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{} satisfies (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi) over all parameters (Theorem 5.3). Algorithm 1 summarizes the combined search–verification loop.

Given the input specification ℐ\mathcal{I} and planner ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p}{}, the algorithm iteratively proposes candidate solutions within a fixed budget δ\delta (Lines 1–4). In each iteration, the planner first synthesizes a set of FGGM definitions 𝒢\mathcal{G} (Line 6), which are then checked for well-formedness using v​a​l​i​d​a​t​e​F​G​G​M{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}validateFGGM} (Line 7). Within 𝒢\mathcal{G}, the planner LLM ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p}{} also synthesizes the prompting functions fpf_{p}{}, enabling each FGGM-specific customization. If the definitions are valid, the planner samples a candidate parametric program 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{} that may invoke these FGGMs (Line 11), and the verification context is extended with their contracts (Line 12). The candidate program is then validated for syntactic correctness, termination, and compliance with the behavioral specification using v​a​l​i​d​a​t​e​P​r​o​g​r​a​m{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}validateProgram} (Line 13). If verification succeeds, the program is returned (Lines 14–15); otherwise, the loop continues with the error feedback until the search budget is exhausted (Lines 16–18).

Theorem 5.3.

If 𝖯{Θ}≠⊥\;\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}\neq\bot with FGGM set 𝒢\mathcal{G}{}, then ∀θ1∈Θ1,…,∀θk∈Θk.φ𝒜⟹(∀x1∈T1,…,∀xn∈Tn.Φ(x1,…,xn)⟹Ψ(x1,…,xn,𝖯{(θ1,…,θk)/Θ}(x1,…,xn)))\forall\theta_{1}\in\Theta_{1},\dots,\forall\theta_{k}\in\Theta_{k}.\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\big(\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\Phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},\mathsf{P}_{\{(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{k})/\Theta\}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\big).

Proof Sketch.

Follows from Theorem 5.2 with details in Appendix R. ∎

5.2.5. Learn

Once a candidate parametric program 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{} passes the search–verification loop (Algorithm 1), the verification step guarantees that 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{} satisfies the behavioral specification (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi) for all parameter values (Theorem 5.3). Hence, the learning step can freely select parameters without violating (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi). Finding the optimal solution to the general formulation in Eq. 19 over {Θ}\{\Theta{}\}{} for a general loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{} is practically intractable. Instead, SEVerA employs a scalable gradient-descent–based optimization to efficiently search over {Θ}\{\Theta{}\}{}.

(19) (θ1∗,…,θk∗)=arg​min(θ1,…,θk)∈{Θ}∑(x,y)∈D𝖫(x,y,𝖯{(θ1,…,θk)/Θ}(x))\displaystyle({\theta_{1}}^{*},\dots,{\theta_{k}}^{*})=\argmin_{(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{k})\in\{\Theta{}\}{}}\;\;{\textstyle\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}{}(x,y,\mathsf{P}_{\{(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{k})/\Theta\}}(x))}

Conformance loss 𝖫Φl,Ψl\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}{} for each local contract (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) encourages the parameters to produce outputs that satisfy their local contracts. By improving conformance with these contracts, SEVerA increases the success rate of the corresponding rejection sampler and thereby avoids triggering the static non-parametric fallback program. Since the fallback cannot be tuned, reducing its usage allows the gradient-based search to more effectively guide the parameters toward solutions that reduce the final loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{}. Our experiments in § 6.3 substantiate this observation, showing that reducing reliance on the fallback improves task performance. For a single FGGM with local contracts (Φl,Ψl)(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}) and parameter θ\theta, we define the conformance loss over an input set ℙ\mathbb{P} in Eq. 20. The inner term 𝖫Φl,Ψlθ​(p)\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}^{\theta}(p) measures the probability that a sampled output from ℒθ​(p)\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(p) violates c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}, while 𝖫Φl,Ψl​(θ)\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}(\theta) aggregates this violation across inputs.

Here, the first term is the task-specific loss over the dataset D\mathrm{D}, and the second term aggregates the local conformance losses (Eq. 20) of the FGGMs appearing in the program. Optimizing all parameters jointly according to Eq. 21, while feasible for smaller neural networks, becomes practically expensive for agents with multiple interdependent LLM calls. To address this challenge, we leverage a key structural property: the conformance loss 𝖫(θi)Φl,Ψli\mathsf{L}{}^{i}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}(\theta_{i}) for each FGGM depends only on the local inputs to that FGGM call and the outputs of its underlying GM, not on the parameters of other FGGMs. This independence arises because each FGGM’s rejection sampler and c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}} checker operate solely on the local contract (Φli,Ψli)(\Phi_{l}^{i},\Psi_{l}^{i}) and the corresponding GM’s outputs. As a result, the conformance term decomposes naturally across FGGM calls. Following this observation, for larger models we approximate the augmented loss by optimizing each FGGM i​dθi{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\theta_{i}}} with parameter θi\theta_{i} independently, as shown in Eq. 22. Here, the first term includes the task-specific loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{} only when the output yly_{l} of i​dθi{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\theta_{i}}} matches the final output yy of the agent on input xx, where (x,_)∈D(x,\_)\in\mathrm{D}. The modularized loss (Eq. 22) enables efficient parallelized training across different θi\theta_{i}.

For generative models with accessible parameters, the objective in Eq. 22 can be optimized using reinforcement learning–based fine-tuning methods such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) (details in Appendix N). Eq. 23 defines the reward for an input-output pair (p,yl)(p,y_{l}), with the goal of learning an output distribution over yly_{l} for inputs p∈ℙp\in\mathbb{P} that maximizes total reward ℛ⁡(p,yl)\mathcal{R}(p,y_{l}). The reward function combines two signals: (1) the task-specific loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{}, which drives the GM toward outputs that reduce overall task error, and (2) the conformance indicator 𝕀⁡(c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl​(p,yl))\mathbb{I}({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(p,y_{l})), which rewards outputs satisfying the local contract. The sigmoid transformation maps the combined penalty to the [0,1][0,1] range, providing a smooth reward landscape. Outputs that violate the local contract receive near-zero reward due to the (1−𝕀⁡(c​h​e​c​k𝒜,Φl,Ψl​(p,yl)))(1-\mathbb{I}({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(p,y_{l}))) penalty term, strongly discouraging the GM from producing outputs that would be rejected by the rejection sampler. The reward function need not be differentiable w.r.t. θi\theta_{i}, as long as the outputs yly_{l} remain differentiable w.r.t. θi\theta_{i} (Shao et al., 2024). For closed-source models with inaccessible parameters, the learning step is skipped, and performance improvements rely solely on prompt tuning through the synthesized fpf_{p} programs within each FGGM.

5.2.6. SEVerA

Algorithm 2 summarizes the overall workflow of SEVerA. The algorithm maintains a pool 𝒫\mathcal{P} of verified candidate agents and iteratively improves it through a search–verify–learn loop. In each iteration, SEVerA first invokes the searchVerify procedure (Algorithm 1), which performs CEGIS-style discrete search to synthesize FGGM definitions and candidate parametric program 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{} that satisfy the behavioral specification (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi). If verification succeeds, the program is passed to the learn procedure, which optimizes the parameters of the underlying generative models using the dataset D\mathrm{D} and task loss 𝖫\mathsf{L}{}. For closed-source models with inaccessible parameters, this step is skipped, and performance improvements rely solely on prompt tuning through the synthesized fpf_{p} programs in each FGGM.

The resulting tuned agent is added to the candidate pool, and its execution traces on D\mathrm{D} are used to construct feedback I′I^{\prime} (see Appendix P) that guides the planner in subsequent search iterations. After the search budget Δ\Delta is exhausted, SEVerA returns the agent in the pool that achieves the lowest task loss on the dataset. If 𝒫\mathcal{P} is empty, SEVerA returns ⊥\bot.

5.3. Theoretical Results

The soundness of SEVerA guarantees that any agent program f∗≠⊥{f}^{*}\neq\bot returned satisfies the behavioral specifications (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi). The searchVerify step generates candidate programs 𝖯{Θ}\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{} that satisfy (Φ,Ψ)(\Phi,\Psi) for all (θ1,…,θk)∈{Θ}(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{k})\in\{\Theta{}\}{}. Consequently, the parameters (θ1∗,…,θk∗)({\theta_{1}}^{*},\dots,{\theta_{k}}^{*}) predicted by the learning step preserve constraint satisfaction. The pool 𝒫\mathcal{P} is either empty or contains only programs that satisfy the behavioral specifications.

Theorem 5.4 (Soundness).

If f∗≠⊥{f}^{*}\neq\bot then, φ𝒜⟹∀x1∈T1,…,∀xn∈Tn.Φ⁡(x1,…,xn)⟹Ψ⁡(x1,…,xn,f∗​(x1,…,xn))\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\Phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},{f}^{*}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})).
